name: Jackson Pr. 13.1: knock-on
description: Jackson Problem 13.1 (energy transfer in a Coulomb collision): throw a heavy ion (pull its slingshot handle back) past the light particle at rest. The ion's field kicks it, the harder the closer the ion passes, $T(b) = T_\text{max}/\left(1 + (b/b_\text{min})^2\right)$: a close pass throws it forward, a distant one sideways. Kick the light particle into its detector, fast enough to count (a gentle push from afar is not a kick).

reality.represents: Energy transfer in a Coulomb collision (Jackson Pr. 13.1)

remarks.detail: The closer the pass, the harder the kick; close passes throw the target forward, distant ones sideways.
A fast ion in matter knocks out electrons thousands of times lighter than itself: the knock-on electrons (δ rays) along particle tracks.
In matter the ion passes many electrons at every distance, and the sum of their kicks is its stopping power (Bethe's formula).

Everything is symmetric about the plane z = 0, so the particle never leaves it. A real beam also has a width across the plane, where the same fields act differently (focusing in the plane can defocus across it).
